Contrast Clues - Part 1

What these questions look like

On the test you will see one sentence with a blank in it. Below it sit four answer choices, and each choice is a whole phrase. Your job is to pick the phrase that best completes the sentence.

How to tackle them

Open each step, then press Continue.

Step 1 - find the signal word

Step 1 - find the signal word

Scan the sentence for a signal word like "although", "despite", or "but".

Step 2 - say what the first part claims

Step 2 - say what the first part claims

Put the first part into your own words. Ask what it claims is true.

Step 3 - flip it, then read the options

Step 3 - flip it, then read the options

Decide what the opposite would sound like before reading any option. Then pick the choice that goes the other way.

Signal word: "although"

How it works

"Although" travels with "even though" and "though", which all work the same way.

"Although" usually sits at the front of the sentence and the words right after it make a claim that will be outweighed. The rest of the sentence, where the blank usually sits, goes the other way.

Example: Although Mia practiced her speech for weeks, she froze on stage.

In this case, the phrase "she froze on stage" goes against the idea presented by the first part of the sentence: "she practiced her speech for weeks". We would typically expect someone who practiced for weeks to do well; instead, Mia froze on stage.

"Although", "even though" and "though" can also appear in the middle of the sentence: Mia froze on stage even though she had practiced her speech for weeks.

Your Turn

Answer correctly to continue.

Signal word: "despite"

How it works

"Despite" works the same way as "in spite of".

"Despite" also usually sits at the front of the sentence, and the words right after it name a thing, not a full statement. You can write "despite the rain" but never "despite it rained", and the rest of the sentence then pushes against that thing.

Example: Despite the loud thunderstorm, the baby slept soundly all night.

In this case, the phrase "the baby slept soundly all night" pushes against the thing named after "despite": "the loud thunderstorm". We would typically expect a loud storm to wake a baby; instead, the baby slept straight through it.

"Despite" can also sit right before the blank, and when it does, the answer you pick must be a thing, not a full statement. It looks like this at the end of the sentence: The picnic went on as planned despite the muddy field.

Your Turn

Answer correctly to continue.

Signal word: "but"

How it works

"But" shares its job with "yet".

"But" is the odd one out because it cannot start the sentence; it sits in the middle instead and works as the turning point. Everything before "but" goes one way, and everything after it goes the other.

Example: The movie's trailer looked thrilling, but the film itself was slow and dull.

In this case, the phrase "the film itself was slow and dull" goes against the first part of the sentence: "the movie's trailer looked thrilling". We would typically expect a thrilling trailer to lead to a thrilling movie; instead, the film turned out slow and dull.

Watch for the shape "not ... but rather ...", which trades one idea for its opposite. It also sits in the middle of the sentence: The desert is not empty, but rather full of hidden life.

Your Turn

Answer correctly to continue.

Watch Out For

  • Do not pick a choice just because it sounds true on its own. Check that it flips the first part.
  • The longest, most detailed choice can look thorough. Extra detail does not make a choice right, so test the flip instead.
  • A choice may repeat a word from the sentence. Matching a word is not the same as matching the meaning.
  • Do not read only the part next to the blank. The signal word usually lives in the first part.

Quick Pattern

Ask yourself: which choice goes the other way from the first part? Decide the flip before you read a single option.
